title: The Art of Statecraft
tagline: Before Machiavelli, there was Chanakya — master of power and strategy.

scenes.text: Northern India, 325 BCE. Alexander the Great has just withdrawn from the subcontinent. The Nanda Empire rules the Gangetic plain with iron taxation and contempt for its people. In Takshashila, the greatest university in the ancient world, a scholar is taking notes.

scenes.speaker: Chanakya
scenes.text: I was humiliated at the Nanda court. Thrown out for my appearance. Very well. I will not ask for their throne — I will build a new one. A kingdom that makes the Nanda look like village chieftains.

challenge.fact: Chanakya is also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta. He served as advisor to Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Empire, and authored the Arthashastra — an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft and political economy.
challenge.instruction: Chanakya is also known by which other name? Learn the phrase and play it back, note for note.

scenes.text: Chanakya found his instrument in a village: a young man named Chandragupta, fierce and clever, with the bearing of a king who did not yet know he was one. For years, Chanakya trained him — strategy, economics, diplomacy, war.

scenes.speaker: Chandragupta
scenes.text: You teach me to play chess against an opponent I have never seen. How can I prepare for every betrayal?

challenge.fact: The Arthashastra (c. 300 BCE) is remarkably pragmatic — Chanakya advises a king to plant spies even in his own court, test ministers with temptations, and treat foreign relations as perpetual competition. Its realpolitik predates Machiavelli's The Prince by nearly 1,800 years.
challenge.instruction: Arrange these priorities from Chanakya's Arthashastra for a new king establishing power: The answer travels in cipher — turn the wheel until it reads.

scenes.speaker: Chanakya
scenes.text: You prepare by understanding human nature. Every minister has a weakness. Greed, pride, fear, love. A king who knows his enemies' weaknesses need not fight every battle — he wins most of them before drawing a sword.

challenge.instruction: Chanakya taught that a king must outmanoeuvre rivals in his own court before facing enemies abroad. Find the decisive move in the council chamber.
challenge.fact: The Arthashastra devotes entire chapters to managing the king's inner circle — testing ministers with planted temptations, using counterintelligence against spies, and playing factions against each other. Chanakya's political realism was as relevant in the Maurya court as in any modern boardroom.

scenes.text: The Arthashastra — Chanakya's treatise on statecraft — covered everything: taxation, law, espionage, agriculture, foreign policy, and the ethics of rule. It was so comprehensive and so ruthlessly pragmatic that Western scholars called him 'the Indian Machiavelli' — though he wrote nearly two thousand years before Machiavelli.

challenge.instruction: Chandragupta must win the loyalty of the Sumerian-descended Mesopotamian governors to consolidate the empire's western border. Sway the council.
challenge.fact: The Maurya Empire under Chandragupta extended westward to meet the successor kingdoms of Alexander the Great. Chanakya's Arthashastra describes in detail how to manage the governors of conquered territories — through a combination of incentives, surveillance, and the projection of royal legitimacy.

scenes.speaker: Chanakya
scenes.text: The Maurya Empire now stretches from the Hindu Kush to the Bay of Bengal. Chandragupta sits on the throne I built for him. My work is done — not as a king, but as the mind behind the king. That is the highest power of all.

challenge.fact: Under Chandragupta Maurya and his grandson Ashoka, the Maurya Empire became one of the largest empires of the ancient world, spanning from modern Afghanistan across the entire subcontinent to Bengal. At its peak under Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE), it covered about 5 million square kilometres — the first political unification of India.
challenge.instruction: The Maurya Empire established by Chanakya and Chandragupta eventually controlled nearly the entire Indian subcontinent. Set the answer in movable type — mirrored, right to left.
The Arthashastra counts war elephants as a kingdom's greatest strength. Guide a wild herd into the stockade — post beaters to close every path out of the forest.
challenge.fact: Seleucus I ceded the Maurya Empire's western provinces to Chandragupta around 303 BCE in return for 500 war elephants. Those elephants helped Seleucus win the Battle of Ipsus two years later — the deal Kautilya's statecraft made possible reshaped the Hellenistic world.
